| [LIT-2479](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2479.md) v3 | COPE - Automating Coupled Evolution of Metamodels and Models | Herrmannsdoerfer, Benz and Juergens (2009), COPE - Automating Coupled Evolution of Metamodels and Models. When a modeling language's metamodel changes, the existing models must be migrated. The paper calls this pairing "coupled evolution". **The requirements study.** An earlier study of two industrial metamodel histories found: - about half the changes were metamodel-only; - more than three quarters of the coupled changes were metamodel-independent, so they could be reused; - the rest were metamodel-specific; - none were model-specific. This yields two requirements: reuse and expressiveness. **COPE's answer.** A language evolves through a sequence of coupled transactions, each pairing a metamodel adaptation with its model migration. There are two kinds: - **Reusable** transactions, drawn from a library: rename, extract class, generalize reference, and so on. - **Custom** transactions, written in a Turing-complete language. | [LIT-2481](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2481.md) v2 | Micropublications: a semantic model for claims, evidence, arguments and annotations in biomedical communications | Clark, Ciccarese and Goble (2014), Micropublications: a semantic model for claims, evidence, arguments and annotations in biomedical communications. The paper treats scientific publications as defeasible arguments and proposes "micropublications" as a layered semantic model, available as an OWL vocabulary at purl.org/mp. **Range of the model.** - At its minimum, a micropublication is a statement with its attribution. - At its maximum, it is a Claim with a support graph of Statements, Data and Methods (including Materials), plus a challenge graph. **Relations and constraints.** - Support is transitive. - A challenge is either direct, or indirect by undercutting a supporter. - Within one micropublication, support forms a DAG rooted at the Claim. - A Representation can be asserted by the micropublication or quoted from another one. This is what lets claim networks span publications. **Contrast with statement-based models.** The paper sets micropublications against nanopublications, SWAN and BEL. Those models represent assertions without their evidence, and they cannot close claim lineages down to data. **Examples.** - Example 4 builds claim networks across papers. - Example 5 handles "similogs" (statements with the same meaning) through holotype claims. - Example 8 models challenge and disagreement. **Citation distortion.** The authors apply the model to Greenberg's case of citation distortion, where a claim was upgraded to "fact" through a chain of self-citations. **Implementation.** It is implemented as a plugin to the Domeo annotation tool. | [LIT-2509](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2509.md) | Git4Voc: Git-based Versioning for Collaborative Vocabulary Development | Lavdim Halilaj, Irlán Grangel-González, Gökhan Coskun and Sören Auer (2016), arXiv 1601.02433. Collaborative vocabulary development is "the process of finding consensus" among experts from different systems; the authors argue that a version control system is "the heart of the problem" and adapt Git. They list eleven requirements (communication, provenance, roles, workflow independence, quality assurance, documentation, deltas between versions, editor independence, modularity, multilinguality, labeled releases) and meet them with conventions and hooks: issues on GitHub-like platforms for discussion; commit history for provenance; a branching model by kind of change (basic, semantic, structural); server- or client-side hooks that enforce roles and run syntax checks (Rapper) and best-practice checks (OOPS!) before a commit, cancelling it on failure; post-commit documentation generation; one triple per line in Turtle so diffs work; files of at most 300 triples as modules; tags for releases. Git cannot show semantic diffs; external tools are proposed.
